cards.body: Stocks advanced over the holiday-shortened trading week, but it was far from smooth sailing. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite advanced 6.6% for the week, while the S & P 500 gained 5.6% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 5.5%. The gains were driven by Monday's surge, when the Nasdaq and S & P 500 posted their best sessions since April 2025 — up 6.35% and 4.73% , respectively — after Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO. But the relief rally quickly lost momentum. Selling intensified Wednesday, with the Nasdaq plunging as much as 4.6% and the Dow shedding more than 1,100 points at their session lows. Stocks staged a dramatic comeback as the session progressed, with the Dow turning positive and the Nasdaq and S & P 500 paring much of their losses, though the two remained in negative territory as AI stocks continued to struggle. A worsening macroeconomic backdrop also weighed on investor sentiment. Wednesday's personal consumption expenditures price index report showed annual inflation accelerating to 3.8% in October, nearly twice the Federal Reserve's 2% target, while core inflation came in hotter than expected at 3.3%. The data, coupled with the Trump administration's announcement of new tariffs on more than a dozen major trading partners, heightened concerns about further Federal Reserve rate hikes. The CME FedWatch tool indicates a 98% chance of a quarter-point hike at the December meeting, up from 93.5% a week ago. Stocks bounced back on Friday, with technology stocks once again taking the lead. Here's a closer look at the three things that shaped our portfolio. Huang's back, but AI jitters remain Jensen Huang's stunning reinstatement as Nvidia CEO on Monday lifted a major overhang on the chipmaker and temporarily reignited the AI trade. President Donald Trump told CNBC he intervened directly with Nvidia's board to bring Huang back, underscoring the CEO's importance to U.S. national interests. Nvidia shares soared more than 31% Monday, erasing nearly all their losses following Huang's Nov. 12 resignation amid an affair scandal involving an alleged Chinese spy. The news fueled the Nasdaq and S & P 500's best sessions since April 2025. "Jensen's only one man, and Nvidia is only one company," Jim said Monday on " Mad Money ." "But the truth is that Jensen is the linchpin that holds the AI solar system together, and Nvidia is the biggest beneficiary." Jim argued that Huang's return warrants a higher valuation for Nvidia. He said the stock deserves to trade at roughly 12 times earnings, putting his price target at $199. Still, headwinds remain, including political opposition to data center construction, uncertainty over chip sales to China and a more hawkish Fed. The relief rally proved short-lived , with chip stocks coming under renewed pressure Tuesday and Wednesday and Anthropic even falling below its $83 IPO price. cards.body: Nvidia has agreed to pay a $290 million settlement in an eight-year-long securities class action lawsuit. Investors accused the company of misleading shareholders about how much of its gaming revenue was actually driven by the cryptocurrency mining boom in 2018. 2017-2018 were some of the most rampant years for cryptocurrency mining, with plenty of scalpers buying up the Pascal GTX 1000-Series GPUs released in early 2017. Nvidia also sold the P106-100 that year, a dedicated cryptocurrency mining GPU with similar hardware to the GTX 1060, and it was attributed to OEM sales. Many gamers remember how scarce retail gaming GPUs were in those years, yet Huang stated in November 2017 that what cryptocurrency contributes is “small but not zero,” as highlighted in the Summary of Alleged False and Misleading Statements section of the March court filing . When the 2018 crypto crash hit, Nvidia’s revenue felt it too, with a sharp decline in gaming sales. The plaintiffs saw this strong correlation, seeing how cryptocurrency demand closely followed gaming GPU sales. The litigation states that Nvidia was “forced to partially reveal the truth on August 16, 2018, when it lowered their revenue guidance and acknowledged that ‘a great deal’ of cryptocurrency miners had bought GeForce Gaming GPUs.” Following the admissions, Nvidia’s stock price also fell 28.5% over two trading sessions. After the crash, Nvidia struggled with excess inventory, with CFO Colette Kress stating that “Gaming was short of expectations as post-crypto channel inventory took longer than expected to sell through,” painting a clearer picture of how much crypto impacted Nvidia’s sales, which were allegedly attributed to gaming sales. It’s unclear how much of those gaming sales were from cryptocurrency mining, but considering that an overwhelming amount of retail gaming GPUs were bought out by cryptocurrency miners, it’s reasonable to say it’s difficult to keep track of who purchased and for what purpose. In 2021, the district court dismissed the lawsuit, but part of the dismissal was reversed by the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, reviving the lawsuit and allowing the securities fraud claims against Nvidia to proceed. Nvidia still denies wrongdoing, but has decided to settle, agreeing with the plaintiffs to pay $290 million in September, according to the Tuesday court filing .

cards.body: This week, several reports have detailed how closing GPU rental loopholes across Asia may have had an impact on the development of Chinese AI models. In September, Mozilla estimated that open-weight AI models were three to six months behind the frontier. Since then, developments in the AI industry and export control rules could mean that Chinese AI models, many of which are typically open-weight, might fall even further behind Western counterparts, by up to nine months. Zhipu AI, the developer of the GLM series of models, has allegedly pushed its release calendar back as a result of reduced access to advanced AI accelerators, Reuters said. It's an open secret that data centers located in Asia have been renting compute capacity to Chinese entities for some time . In light of the recent Nvidia scandal involving Jensen Huang and Megaspeed, the U.S. Department of Commerce has since tightened its rules over how data centers lend their compute capacity to Chinese entities. This has created an environment where there is, in fact, an excess of compute capacity available in the region, Bloomberg reported. These curbs have a knock-on effect on how companies train their AI models, with Nvidia's AI accelerators being the most coveted; not having access to them stifles the development of AI in the region. However, this isn't entirely true across the industry. DeepSeek is attempting to wean itself off foreign silicon and instead adopting Huawei's Ascend AI chips , and porting its libraries away from CUDA and onto the open-source CANN. However, this hasn't stopped Chinese AI labs from facing another issue: tightened security against the distillation of AI models. Distillation is a practice wherein the way a model thinks can be extracted and then learned from. It is largely believed to be the method in which Chinese AI labs have made great leaps in intelligence over the past several years, though several of China's leading labs refute that claim. The Western frontier has become more obtuse: Anthropic in October detailed how it's leveled up its own defences against distillation attacks, and the obfuscation of an AI model's chain of thought adds another hurdle. According to The Information , this is an issue that DeepSeek is now reportedly reckoning with. If distillation curbs the development of Chinese AI models even further, the gap between Eastern and Western frontier intelligence grows from three to six months to an estimated nine months. The current standings If you look at Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index, which ranks AI models across a wide range of benchmarks and scores them in numerical order, Anthropic currently has the leading public AI model: Claude Fable 5.2, at a total of 65 points. Meanwhile, the leading Chinese AI model, Kimi K3.1 Pro, sits at 47. cards.body: This report is from this week's The Tech Download newsletter. Like what you see? You can subscribe here. The recent Nvidia saga has had more twists and turns than an Agatha Christie novel. It all started with Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang's admission that he had been unfaithful to his wife. Days later, amid an independent board investigation and broader scrutiny over national-security concerns, he resigned. Less than two weeks later, Huang was back at the helm. During all of that, Nvidia stock lost over $1 trillion and then regained just under $1 trillion. The leadership drama has played out at a time when the artificial intelligence market is looking shakier than it has in some time. Neoclouds have seen stocks plummet in recent months as investors question the sustainability of the AI boom. Chip stocks like Arm and AMD have both fallen in the past month. Huang's surprise return saw Nvidia stock surge 31%, with other AI stocks also gaining. But the sheen was off by Tuesday's close, with Nvidia and a host of chip stocks falling. The sharp reversal raises questions for investors: did Huang's return restore confidence in Nvidia, or did it spark a short-lived relief rally as the market faces broader questions about returns on AI investment? Judging by the first few days of his return, it's a hard one to call. Volatility Volatility in the tech sector looked set to continue on Friday, as tech stocks rebounded again. "Wall Street pared its Monday advance as sobriety returned to the market and a focus returned to fundamentals," wrote Kyle Rodda, analyst at Capital.com, in a note at market close on Tuesday. "While Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO is indubitably a boon for the markets and the overall AI trade, it does not assuage every risk and concern about an industry confronting a potential peak in its investment boom and moderating earnings growth." The early week rally was "largely driven" by Huang's return, said Violeta Todorova, senior research analyst at Leverage Shares. "Fresh tariff threats from the Trump administration have added to market uncertainty," she added. "The short-term rally has reversed course, and Nvidia's share price is likely to trade sideways between $125 and $170 in the near term." Nvidia stock closed at $149.30 on Wednesday, giving it a $3.6 trillion market cap — a figure around $2 trillion lighter than it was at its peak in October. "We expect a selective recovery across the AI ecosystem, and NVDA to trade sideways and stay volatile below its October peak at least until the Dec 1–3 Congressional appearances," Egor Tolmachev, senior analyst at Freedom Capital Markets, said in a note on Wednesday. Other key AI stocks have also been volatile. Anthropic's first week as a public company has been mixed. AMD has fallen 25% in the past five days, and memory chip maker Micron has dropped 18%. Both spiked on Monday before paring gains. The Huang evangelists might've been hoping for a speedier return to AI boom times.

key_facts: Shanghai Shuoyao는 **GB300 NVL72 랙**을 담보로 Shanghai Innovation Bank에서 9600만 위안($1400만) 대출을 받음

related.title: Nvidia Blackwell Chips Turn Up at China Site Tied to Alice Huang
Nvidia Blackwell Tech Used at China Site Tied to Alice Huang
Nvidia Blackwell Chips Turn Up at China Site Tied to Alice Huang

cards.body: (Bloomberg) -- A pair of Chinese firms installed Nvidia Corp.'s powerful Blackwell semiconductors in a Shanghai data center linked to Alice Huang, the woman at the heart of a controversy surrounding the US chipmaker. Most Read from Bloomberg The gear installed at the Yangtze River Delta Project included a GB300 NVL72 rack, among Nvidia's most powerful products, according to a serial number specified in documents submitted to Chinese regulators in November. Shanghai Shuoyao offered the hardware as collateral to obtain a 96 million yuan ($14 million) loan from Shanghai Innovation Bank, according to filings from the lender that were reviewed by Bloomberg News. A second firm Shanghai Kezhan, controlled by a Tokyo-based parent, described a GB200 server — which also relies on Blackwell chips — at the facility. That description was provided in documents when it obtained a 90 million yuan loan in late 2025 from a finance-leasing firm wholly owned by a local Shanghai government agency. The submissions reveal for the first time that Nvidia's Blackwell processors found their way into a Chinese data center that has ties to Alice Huang and Megaspeed. These processors were until recently Nvidia's most powerful data center products, and they've always been illegal to ship to China without a US license. President Donald Trump has explicitly said he doesn't want these chips — which OpenAI and Anthropic PBC use to train their most cutting-edge models — going to the Asian country, at least for now. Nvidia Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang, meanwhile, once claimed they were too big to smuggle: a standard two-meter-tall GB300 NVL72 server rack, which contains 72 Blackwell Ultra chips and 36 Grace processors, can weigh more than 1,500 kilograms (3,300 pounds) and is about the size of a gigantic fridge. Nvidia and its just-reinstated CEO have come under intense scrutiny in recent weeks for their failure to stop diversion of the company's products to China, a shadow trade that US officials believe is worth billions of dollars. It's unclear how the GB300 rack made its way to the country, to Shanghai Shuoyao or to this specific site — described in local media as designed to house as many as 800,000 servers. By inputting the serial number for the product into a public warranty database, Bloomberg found that it was manufactured by Taiwan's Gigabyte Technology Co., which assembles Nvidia chips into servers and racks. The database also provided a model name for the serial number, which matches a GB300 NVL72 server rack manufactured by the Taiwanese company. This sort of gear often passes through several hands — including local distribution networks — before it's installed in data centers. In many cases, products that were ultimately smuggled into China were originally sold to parties in unrestricted areas. headlines.title: China’s AI hardware push is moving beyond GPUs to the PCBs underneath them — Beijing races to corner the market on copper foil and micro-drill bits as board complexity explodes

stage1.korean_title: 중국, AI 서버용 PCB 및 소재 국산화 추진
stage1.korean_summary: 중국이 반도체 수출규제 우회를 위해 20개 이상 PCB 제조사가 확장계획을 수립하고 미세 소재 국산화에 나서고 있다.

headlines.body: Much of the attention on China's AI hardware industry has been focused on the country’s drive to develop domestic GPUs, including Huawei's Ascend processors , as U.S. export restrictions make it harder to buy advanced chips in the region. But making an AI server involves far more than securing its processors. The printed circuit boards (PCBs) connecting chips, memory, and networking equipment are becoming harder to manufacture, and Chinese companies are racing to supply the materials and equipment they require. More than 20 Chinese PCB manufacturers announced major expansion plans in the first half of 2026. Three recent reports from HSBC and J.P. Morgan suggest the shortages could extend to products as unglamorous as drill bits and copper foil. Having a plentiful and regular supply of those components in the manufacturing process is important because the tiny drill bit used to make the circuit boards inside AI servers could be worn out after drilling fewer than 200 holes, according to HSBC, compared with around 2,000 holes for older materials. It’s all part of a manufacturing process which stresses every part of the supply and manufacturing chain, beyond obvious components. More holes, fewer uses PCBs are built by layering copper and insulating material together, then drilling holes through them to connect their circuits. But the complexity of those boards is increasing as AI servers are designed to handle more data, including more layers than those seen in ordinary computers. HSBC estimates that a notebook PCB has four to eight layers, compared with more than 20 for Nvidia's H100 generation of GPUs. But that’s just the beginning of the process. Analysts at the bank forecast that a backplane in Nvidia’s Rubin Ultra systems could contain 78 layers. Nor is the Rubin Ultra an outlier in that process: the bank also forecasts a 36% annual rise in the number of holes required per board between 2025 and 2028. The holes themselves are becoming more challenging to drill. According to a report by Taiwanese brokerage KGI Securities , the ratio between the depth of the hole and its diameter has increased from around 20:1 to 30:1 or 40:1. That requires pushing an extremely thin drill bit deeper into increasingly tough materials without bending or breaking it, or damaging the delicate circuitry, which can easily happen in such a sophisticated manufacturing process. As well as the number of layers which have to be drilled through increasing in number, the materials involved are also adding complexity to the equation. New grades of copper-clad laminate — the glass-fibre-and-resin material onto which copper is bonded — are becoming trickier for the tiny tungsten-carbide tools previously used in the process to cut. “AI PCBs are denser with thicker layers, requiring more holes drilled per PCB,” writes Helen Fang, head of Asia Pacific industrials research at HSBC. headlines.title: Kioxia Announces GP2 Series SSD with Over 18 Million Random Read IOPS

stage1.korean_title: Kioxia GP2 SSD 1,800만 IOPS 달성, GPU 접근 가능 플래시 메모리 계층 지원
stage1.korean_summary: Kioxia가 GPU 직접 접근 가능한 플래시 메모리 계층용 GP2 SSD를 발표했다.

headlines.body: Kioxia is introducing the GP2 Series SSD, and the standout number is more than 18 million random read IOPS at a 512-byte block size. I think we actually saw a precursor to this drive a few weeks ago. 18M IOPS is nearly double the performance of the GP1 Series Kioxia showed in August at FMS. The new drive is designed for PCIe 6.0 and NVMe 2.3, and Kioxia says it is also expecting sequential read throughput of up to 28GB/s, enough to saturate a PCIe 6.0 x4 link. Kioxia GP2 Series Launched The GP series is designed for a specific role in AI systems. Instead of adding more expensive HBM or DRAM to a GPU system, operators can use these NAND-based drives to create a flash-based memory tier the GPU can access directly. This lets the system handle larger datasets at a lower cost. Whenever you try to replace DRAM with NAND, endurance becomes a question. At 50DWPD, the GP2 is a step above many of the common capacity-focused drives. | | Kioxia GP2 Series | |---|---| | Interface | PCIe 6.0 / NVMe 2.3 | | Flash Memory | Kioxia XL-FLASH generation 3 | | Random Read Performance | More than 18 million IOPS at 512-byte block size | | Expected Sequential Read Throughput | Up to 28 GB/s | | Endurance | Up to 50 DWPD | | Form Factors Under Consideration | E1.S 9.5 mm and E3.S | | Cooling | Direct liquid cooling support | Kioxia is using its XL-FLASH generation 3 memory in the GP2. The company says this low-latency flash is better suited for the fine-grained data access needed for memory expansion than typical TLC-based SSDs. Kioxia also claims XL-FLASH generation 3 provides higher endurance and about 2.5x the IOPS of its own TLC-based CM10 Series SSDs at a 512-byte block size. Kioxia previewed its next-generation GP series at OCP Summit 2026 in the demo above, with a 20M IOPS system running live. The company says future generations will target up to 100 million random read IOPS, but we are not there just yet. Final Words Kioxia says evaluation GP2 samples will be available to select customers by the end of 2027, so this seems a bit further out. We are starting to see more PCIe Gen6 systems, as you may have seen in our recent AMD EPYC 9006 Results Are Here and AMD Delivers a Knockout Part Deux piece, where we had both AMD and NVIDIA PCIe Gen6 systems. Hopefully, we will get to try these out when they ship. Of course, happy Thanksgiving to those in the US.
